title: The broken dam
hook: the people of Sheba are given two gardens, turn away, and the dam bursts (34:15–17)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sulayman, whose death only a small creature knew. Your line was only the termite knew.

Nobody thanks a light switch. A gift that works every day goes invisible. Surah thirty-four carries the name of a people, Saba', Sheba, whose gift was water, held back and shared out across their fields. Near Ma'rib in Yemen, old stone ruins of a dam still stand, and commentators connect them with this story. The surah tells it in three short verses, and it isn't really about engineering at all.

Verse fifteen. There was a sign for Sheba in their homeland: two gardens, one on the right and one on the left. The instruction that came with them is short. Pickthall: "Eat of the provision of your Lord and render thanks to Him. A fair land and an indulgent Lord!" That last line is almost a postcard: a good land, and a Lord who forgives. Verse sixteen: but they turned away. So Allah sent on them sayl al-'arim, the flood of the dam, or as some translate it, the overwhelming flood. Their two gardens were exchanged for gardens of bitter fruit, tamarisk, and a few lote trees. Verse seventeen gives the reason in one word: kafaru, they were ungrateful. Classical dictionaries connect the root, k-f-r, with covering over. Ingratitude covers a gift, like soil over a seed, until you stop seeing it. The Qur'an doesn't list a dramatic crime. Nobody told them to do anything hard. Eat, and give thanks: that was the whole instruction, and it was the thanks they let go. Commentators connect the burst dam with the dam at Ma'rib; the Qur'an itself doesn't give a date or name the dam. It names the pattern: a gift received without gratitude starts to come apart, and what replaces it is thin and bitter. A few verses earlier, about Dawud's family, the same surah says it plainly: few of Allah's servants are thankful.

If you can, pour a glass of water and hold it, and think about where it came from: rain, a river, a reservoir, a pipe someone laid. Take a slow sip. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah, the praise belongs to God, as many Muslims do after drinking; if not, simply notice the gift in your hand.
Sheba, the people with two gardens and every provision, whose own ingratitude brought the flood that broke their dam. Today's word.
Your line: gratitude keeps the garden. Two gardens, and one small instruction. Day five hundred forty-five, done.

howItsDone: Many Muslims say bismillah before drinking and alhamdulillah after, and scholars often cite the story of Sheba when teaching that gratitude (shukr) preserves blessings.

fork.setup: you live in Sheba. two gardens, a fair land, a forgiving Lord. you're asked only to eat and give thanks. what did Sheba do?
options: gave thanks, and kept the gardens.
fork.reveal: they turned away, and the flood of the dam came. the Qur'an's one word for why is ingratitude.

original.note: Arabic: the flood of al-'arim, often read as the dam, or the overwhelming flood.

what it means: a people given everything, asked only for thanks, who turned away until the gift came apart.
what a scholar hears: kafaru in 34:17 shares the root k-f-r, covering over; commentators tie sayl al-'arim to the Ma'rib dam in Yemen.

chat.says: What went wrong for the people of Sheba in the Qur'an?
options: They were told to eat and give thanks, and they let the thanks go.
They built their dam badly, and the Qur'an blames their engineers.
They chased trade so far that they abandoned their two gardens.
chat.meaning: Saba' 34:15–17: two gardens and one instruction, eat and give thanks. They turned away; the verse's word is kafaru, they were ungrateful.

Sheba.meaning: Saba', a people whose homeland had two gardens

Ma'rib.meaning: a place in Yemen with old dam ruins

kafaru.meaning: they were ungrateful; from a root linked to covering

sayl al-'arim.meaning: the flood of the dam, or the overwhelming flood
